title: Two ears, hands free: Mercadier’s bi-telephone
summary: An 1891 patent documents paired ear receivers held by a resilient yoke.
problem: The patent addresses securing telephone receivers while leaving the operator’s hands free.
solution: Two receiver housings attach to a spring-like support; rubber-covered earpieces sit at the ears.
significance: This is direct evidence of a wearable, two-ear electrical listening design before Baldwin’s later devices.
uncertainty: A patent grant dates a documented design. It does not prove the first invention, commercial adoption or stereo reproduction.

title: Baldwin’s Type C in the museum record
summary: A surviving Type C headset connects headphone history to radio communication.
problem: Radio and communication are the contexts recorded by the museum; the maker’s personal motivation is not established here.
solution: The Henry Ford preserves a Baldwin Radio Company headset made in Salt Lake City, dated 1915–1920.
significance: The object gives the timeline a physical reference, rather than relying on a single-inventor origin story.
uncertainty: Its inscriptions cite patents dated 1910 and 1915. Those dates are distinct from the museum’s manufacture range.

title: Stereo music becomes a headphone proposition
summary: Koss dates the SP/3 stereophone to 1958.
problem: Koss’s retrospective places the device within a stereo phonograph demonstration.
solution: John C. Koss and Martin Lange Jr. developed a portable stereo record player; the SP/3 became part of this music-listening story.
significance: The milestone shifts the timeline’s focus from communication to personal stereo music.
uncertainty: Koss calls it the first stereo headphone. We attribute that priority claim to the manufacturer rather than treating it as independently settled.

title: An open-back milestone: HD 414
summary: Sennheiser dates the launch of its HD 414 open-back headphones to 1968.
problem: The documented innovation concerns enclosure design, not a new recording format.
solution: The HD 414 introduced an open headphone construction in Sennheiser’s product history.
significance: It is a useful historical anchor for understanding open-back designs in today’s catalogue.
uncertainty: The world-first claim is Sennheiser’s account. This entry does not independently resolve all earlier experimental designs.

title: Stereo leaves the living room: TPS-L2
summary: Sony’s first-generation Walkman went on sale in July 1979.
problem: Portable personal listening is the context of this milestone; no undocumented inventor motivation is assumed.
solution: The TPS-L2 paired a portable cassette player with headphone listening. Sony records different early overseas product names.
significance: The entry connects portable sources to the role of headphones in everyday listening.
uncertainty: July 1979 refers to the initial launch, not every regional release. The Walkman did not invent headphones.

title: A new wireless audio specification family
summary: Bluetooth SIG announced completion of the LE Audio specification suite on 12 July 2022.
problem: The standard addresses audio delivery over Bluetooth Low Energy.
solution: LE Audio defines a new audio architecture, including the LC3 codec and multi-stream capabilities.
significance: It creates a standards milestone for later compatible headphones and source devices.
uncertainty: Specification completion is not a product launch. A Bluetooth version number alone does not establish LE Audio support.
